title: Investigate using logs, metrics and traces
description: Project: Investigate using logs, metrics and traces. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: When an incident fires, your job is to answer three questions fast: What happened, why did it happen, and who is affected. Logs, metrics, and traces are the three signals that answer different parts of that question. This lesson shows how to use them together during an investigation, how to correlate them with trace IDs, and how to avoid the common trap of looking at one signal in isolation.

items: Metrics tell you when something changed: error rate spiked, latency p99 doubled, saturation hit 90 percent
Logs tell you why it changed: exception messages, authorization failures, database timeouts, configuration errors
Traces tell you where in the distributed path the slowdown or error occurred: which downstream service, which span, which retry loop
Correlation IDs tie metrics, logs, and traces together so one incident ID surfaces all three views
Dashboards reduce context switching by showing the three signals side by side on a single pane

terms.definition: A unique identifier attached to a request that flows through all services, logs, and traces, enabling end-to-end correlation.
A single unit of work within a trace, representing one operation such as an HTTP call or database query.
Metadata that propagates across service boundaries alongside a trace, such as user ID or tenant ID.
Logs emitted as JSON objects with typed fields for reliable filtering, aggregation, and correlation.
A metrics framework focusing on Request rate, Error rate, and Duration for every service.

data.text: The fastest investigations start with metrics. Metrics tell you the blast radius and when the change began. Once you know the affected service and time window, use logs to identify the specific error, then use traces to show the full request path that led to it. Starting with logs is like searching a haystack; starting with metrics narrows the haystack first.

items: Identify the alert and the affected metric from your on-call dashboard
Confirm the time window and whether the change is ongoing or resolved
Query logs for the affected service and time window using structured filters
Use trace ID or correlation ID from the logs to pull the full distributed trace
Identify the failing span, the error message, and any retry or timeout behavior
Form a hypothesis and verify it against metrics, logs, and traces before taking action

data.title: Correlate early, correlate always
data.text: Inject trace IDs and correlation IDs at the edge of your system. If you wait until an incident to add correlation, you have already lost the data you need. Every log line, metric label, and trace span should carry the same request identifier.

items: Jumping to a fix after reading one error log without checking the trace for root cause
Ignoring metrics that show the issue started before the error logs appeared
Correlating traces manually by timestamp instead of by trace ID
Trusting logs without verifying the timestamp is synchronized across services
Over-relying on sampling; the failing request may not be in the sampled trace set

items.question: What if the failing request was not traced?
items.answer: Increase the sampling rate for error paths or use head-based sampling with a tail-based sampler that keeps all traces for errors. If you cannot reconstruct the trace, use logs with correlation IDs to approximate the request path.

items.question: How do I correlate logs and traces in Loki?
items.answer: Use the same trace ID field in both your structured logs and your trace exporter. Grafana Tempo can query Loki for logs matching a specific trace ID if the labels are aligned.

items.question: Should I use OpenTelemetry or vendor-specific SDKs?
items.answer: Prefer OpenTelemetry for new instrumentation. It avoids vendor lock-in and supports automatic instrumentation for .NET, Node.js, and most common frameworks. Vendor SDKs may offer deeper integration but trap you in their ecosystem.

data.title: Investigate a simulated latency spike
data.description: You receive an alert: p99 latency for the checkout service increased from 200ms to 3 seconds. Use metrics, logs, and traces to find the root cause within 15 minutes.
steps: Open the metrics dashboard and confirm the time window and affected endpoint
Query logs for 500 errors in the same window
Extract a trace ID from the logs and view the full trace
Identify the slow span and explain why it is slow
Propose a fix and write a brief incident update
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce a clear root cause hypothesis supported by all three signals, plus a concrete remediation step.

data.title: Summary
points: Start with metrics to scope the blast radius and time window
Use logs to find the specific error message and affected request
Use traces to show the full request path and identify the slow span
Correlate all signals with trace IDs and correlation IDs
Form a hypothesis before taking action; verify it against all three signals
data.takeaway: A senior engineer treats logs, metrics, and traces as three views of the same incident, not as separate systems. Correlation is the skill that turns raw signals into a clear root cause.
